decisions.title: Memory Separated into Typed Buckets
decisions.description: Memory records are classified into types: user preferences, project constraints, environment facts, and session observations. Each type has its own persistence and retrieval rules. User preferences survive across projects; project constraints are scoped to one codebase; session observations are temporary. This typing prevents the common failure mode where everything gets dumped into one memory store and retrieval becomes noisy.
decisions.alternatives: A single flat memory store is simpler but makes retrieval imprecise. Storing everything as natural language text and relying on semantic search works at scale but adds embedding infrastructure.

decisions.title: Load Memory Before Prompt Assembly, Write After Work
decisions.description: The memory lifecycle has two clear moments: load relevant memory right before assembling the prompt, and extract and persist new memory after the agent finishes its work. This split ensures memory always flows in the right direction -- old context informs new work, new work updates the durable record. Loading too early means stale data; writing too early means incomplete observations.
decisions.alternatives: Loading memory at session start and writing at session end is simpler but misses mid-session updates. Continuous background sync is more real-time but adds complexity and potential race conditions.

decisions.title: Memory and Context Are Different State Containers
decisions.description: Short-term messages[] carries the live conversation process. Compacted summaries carry compressed session history. Long-term memory carries cross-session facts that cannot be re-derived. These three containers have different lifespans, different sizes, and different access patterns. Mixing them up leads to either context bloat (stuffing memory into messages) or amnesia (compressing away facts that should be permanent).
decisions.alternatives: Treating all state as one conversation history simplifies the model but causes context overflow. Storing everything in long-term memory and retrieving on demand sounds clean but adds latency and retrieval uncertainty to every turn.
